3.        Common questions of law arising for consideration in all these appeals

are:

          (i)     Whether Section 292BB of the Income Tax Act, 19611 precludes
                  an Assessee from raising an objection in any proceedings under
                  the Act regarding non-service of a notice under Section 143(2)
                  of the Act, if the Assessee had appeared and cooperated during
                  the reassessment proceedings and had not raised any objection
                  with regard to non-issuance of a notice under Section 143(2) of
                  the Act? and

          (ii)    Whether an Assessee who requests that the earlier Return of
                  Income filed under Section 139 of the Act be treated as the
                  Return of Income filed in response to a notice under Section 148
                  of the Act is not required to be given a notice under Section
                  143(2) of the Act?, and

          (iii)   Whether a letter given by the Assessing Officer during the course
                  of reassessment proceedings, requiring the Assessee to explain
                  the grounds on which re-assessment of income was proposed,
                  would tantamount to sufficient compliance of the provision of

              Section 143(2) of the Act?

4.     In all these appeals, the Assessees had filed the respective Returns of

their Income for the respective Assessment years under Section 139 of the Act,

which were duly assessed, and assessment orders passed under Section 143(3)

of the Act. Subsequently, the Revenue sought to reopen the assessments under

Section 147 of the Act and issued notices under Section 148 of the Act,

requiring the assesses to file the returns in the prescribed form.


5.     In the case of Orissa Mining Corporation Ltd., the Assessee filed a

response stating that its Return of Income originally filed under Section 139

of the Act, be treated as the Return of Income in response to a notice under

Section 148 of the Act. In the case of Bijoy Kishore Mohanty, it is stated that

the same Return of Income which had earlier been filed under Section 139 of

the Act, was refiled in response to the notice issued under Section 148 of the

Act.


6.     Thereafter, admittedly no notice under section 143(2) of the Act was

issued and the reassessment proceedings were commenced. During the

reassessment proceedings, and notices under Section 142(1) of the Act were

issued to the Assessee, seeking documents/stock information to be submitted.


7.     Pursuant thereto, the reassessment orders were framed against the


                                        3
Assessees, which were challenged by the Assessees by approaching the

Appellate Authority, i.e., Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals). One of the

grounds raised by the Assessee before the Appellate Authority was with regard

to failure of the Revenue to issue a notice under Section 143(2) of the Act,

thereby vitiating the entire proceedings.


8.    Appellate Authority rejected the argument of the Assessee with regards

to vitiation of the proceedings on account of failure of the Revenue to serve a

notice under Section 143(2) of the Act. Appellate Authority held that since the

Assessees had participated in the assessment proceedings after the issuance of

a notice under Section 148, followed by a notice under Section 142(1), the

Assessees could not be allowed to raise the ground of non-issuance of a notice

under Section 143(2) of the Act at the appellate stage.


9.    Aggrieved therefrom, the Assesses approached the Income Tax

Appellate Tribunal. In the respective cases, the Appellate Tribunal held that

the assessment proceedings stood vitiated for want of notice under Section

143(2) of the Act and, thus, set aside the reassessment orders.


10.   Aggrieved by the decisions of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, the

Revenue challenged the respective orders before the High Court. The High

Court had rejected the challenge, and upheld the orders of Income Tax


                                       4
Appellate Tribunal, confirming that the assessment proceedings were vitiated

on the ground of failure of the authority to issue a notice under Section 143(2)

of the Act.


11.   Section 143 of the Act reads as under:

      “143. (1) Where a return has been made under section 139, or in
      response to a notice under sub-section (1) of section 142, such
      return shall be processed in the following manner, namely: —

      *******

      (2)     Where a return has been furnished under section 139, or in
      response to a notice under sub-section (1) of section 142, the
      Assessing Officer or the prescribed income-tax authority, as the
      case may be, if, considers it necessary or expedient to ensure that
      the Assessee has not understated the income or has not computed
      excessive loss or has not under-paid the tax in any manner, shall
      serve on the Assessee a notice requiring him, on a date to be
      specified therein, either to attend the office of the Assessing Officer
      or to produce, or cause to be produced before the Assessing
      Officer any evidence on which the Assessee may rely in support of
      the return:

      Provided that no notice under this sub-section shall be served on
      the Assessee after the expiry of three months from the end of the
      financial year in which the return is furnished.

      (3)     On the day specified in the notice issued under sub-section
      (2), or as soon afterwards as may be, after hearing such evidence
      as the Assessee may produce and such other evidence as the

                                        5
         Assessing Officer may require on specified points, and after taking
         into account all relevant material which he has gathered, the
         Assessing Officer shall, by an order in writing, make an
         assessment of the total income or loss of the Assessee, and
         determine the sum payable by him or refund of any amount due to
         him on the basis of such assessment:

         Provided that ********

         (4) ******”

12.      Section 143(2) of the Act mandates service of a notice on the Assessee,

requiring him to attend the office of the Assessing Officer or to produced

before the Assessing Officer any evidence on which the Assessee may rely in

support of the return. This Court, in Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax

and Another vs. Hotel Blue Moon2 has held that the omission on the part of

the Assessing Authority to issue a notice under Section 143(2) of the act

cannot be treated as a procedural irregularity that is curable, and therefore, the

requirement of issuing a notice under Section 143(2) of the Act cannot be

dispensed with.


13.      This Court, in Hotel Blue Moon (supra) has specifically laid down that

where the Assessing Officer intends to make an enquiry, he must necessarily

follow the provisions of Section 142 and Section 143(2) & 143(3) of the Act.



2
    (2010) 3 SCC 259

                                         6
A notice under Section 143(2) of the Act is mandatory, as it grants the

Assessee an opportunity to produce or cause to be produced any evidence or

particulars based on which the Assessee claims relief. A notice under section

143(2) of the Act is sine qua non for a proceeding for reassessment under

Section 147 of the Act. In the absence of a notice under Section 143(2) of the

Act, no further proceedings can be undertaken by the Revenue.


14.    In the present case, admittedly no notice under Section 143(2) of the

Act was admittedly issued. The excuse given by the Revenue is that such a

notice was not required to be given and failure to give such a notice is not fatal

to the reassessment proceedings. Reliance is placed by the Revenue on the

provision of Section 292BB of the Act, which reads as under:-


       “292BB. Notice deemed to be valid in certain circumstances.

       Where an Assessee has appeared in any proceeding or co-operated
       in any inquiry relating to an assessment or reassessment, it shall
       be deemed that any notice under any provision of this Act, which
       is required to be served upon him, has been duly served upon him
       in time in accordance with the provisions of this Act and such
       Assessee shall be precluded from taking any objection in any
       proceeding or inquiry under this Act that the notice was—

       (a) not served upon him; or

       (b) not served upon him in time; or



                                        7
      (c) served upon him in an improper manner:

      Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply where
      the Assessee has raised such objection before the completion of
      such assessment or reassessment.”

15.   Section 292BB creates a deeming fiction in respect of any proceedings

in which an Assessee had appeared or an inquiry in which the Assessee

cooperated relating to assessment or reassessment. The deeming fiction

stipulates that any notice required to be served upon the Assessee, under the

provision of the Act, shall be deemed to have been duly served upon him in

time and in accordance with the provisions of the Act, and the Assessee is

precluded from taking any objection that the notice was either not served upon

him, or not served upon him in time, or served upon him in an improper

manner. Said provision precludes an Assessee from raising an objection with

regards to service, timely service and proper service of a notice which is

required to be served upon him. Such a deeming fiction can come into play

only if notice is alleged to have been sent by the Revenue.


16.   Only when the Revenue contends that a notice, as required under the

Act has been sent, the Assessee who has participated in the proceedings or

inquiry relating to assessment or reassessment, pursuant to the notice would

be precluded from taking any objection that the notice was not served upon

him, or was not served in time, or that the service of notice was not proper.

                                      8
Said deeming fiction cannot come into play where the Revenue has admittedly

not even issued the notice. Where the Revenue itself contends that no notice

was sent, as required under the Act, the provision of Section 292BB will have

no applicability.


17.    The Assessing Officer cannot undertake the proceedings of

reassessment under Section 143(3), read with Section 147 of the Act, unless a

notice under Section 143(2) of the Act has been issued to the Assessee. Mere

participation of the Assessee in the assessment proceedings, in the absence of

a notice under Section 143(2) of the Act, does not confer jurisdiction on the

Assessing Officer to frame an assessment under Section 143 (3) of the Act.


18.    Furthermore, in response to a notice issued under Section 148 of the

Act, requiring the Assessee to file a Return of Income in the prescribed format,

the Assessee has the option to file a fresh Return of Income. In case the

Assessee does not wish to file a fresh Return of Income and seeks to rely upon

the Return of Income filed earlier under Section 139 of the Act, it is open to

the Assessee, in response to the notice under section 148 of the Act, to merely

state that its earlier Return of Income be treated as the Return of Income in

response to the notice and he remains bound by it. If the Assessee seeks to

reiterate its earlier Return of Income, it is not necessary for the Assessee to

refile a copy of its earlier Return of Income. In the present case, the Assessees

                                       9
have chosen not to file a fresh return and have reiterated their Return of Income

already filed, Thus, the obligation on the Revenue to issue a notice under

Section 143(2) of the Act, requiring the Assessee to produce evidence on

which the Assessee seeks to rely on in support of the Return of Income, cannot

be dispensed with.


19.    Furthermore, Section 143(3) of the Act empowers the Assessing

Officer to make an assessment after hearing such evidence as the Assessee

may produce and such evidence as the Assessing Officer may require on

specified points, pursuant to the notice issued under Section 143(2) of the Act.


20.    Admittedly, in the present case, no notice issued under Section 143(2)

of the Act was issued to the Assessee for the respective assessment years.

Consequently, in terms of the law laid down by this Court in Hotel Blue Moon

(supra), the Assessing Officer could not have framed the assessments, and as

such the proceedings are vitiated. As held in Hotel Blue Moon (supra), the

omission on the part of the Assessing Authority to issue a notice under Section

143(2) of the Act is not a mere procedural irregularity and is not curable.


21.    Furthermore, mere participation in the proceedings by the Assessees

does not come to the aid of the Revenue in terms of the Section 292BB of the

Act. Reference has been made to the judgment of this Court in Commissioner


                                       10
of Income Tax vs. Laxman Das Khandelwal3, wherein this Court has held

that the scope of Section 292BB is to make service of notice, having certain

infirmities, to be proper and valid, if there was requisite participation on the

part of the Assessee. It does not save complete absence of notice and non-

issuance of notice under Section 143(2) of the act by the Revenue, and will

make the entire proceedings invalid.


22.      A letter given by the Assessing Officer under section 142 (1)4 of the


3
    (2021) 18 SCC 691
4
    Inquiry before assessment.

142. (1) For the purpose of making an assessment under this Act, the Assessing Officer
may serve on any person who has made a return under section 115WD or section 139
or in whose case the time allowed under sub-section (1) of section 139 for furnishing
the return has expired a notice requiring him, on a date to be therein specified, —

(i) *****

(ii) to produce, or cause to be produced, such accounts or documents as the Assessing
Officer may require, or

(iii) to furnish in writing and verified in the prescribed manner information in such
form and on such points or matters (including a statement of all assets and liabilities
of the assessee, whether included in the accounts or not) as the Assessing Officer may
require:

Provided that—********

(2) For the purpose of obtaining full information in respect of the income or loss of any
person, the Assessing Officer may make such inquiry as he considers necessary.

*******

                                           11
Act during the course of reassessment proceedings would not satisfy the

requirements of a notice under section 143(2) of the Act. A notice under

section 143(2) of the Act is a sine qua non for commencing the proceedings.

A letter issued after commencing the proceedings would not cover up the

lacuna in the proceedings and would not validate what is non est.


23.     In view of the above, we find no infirmity in the view taken by the

Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, as affirmed by the High Court. The question

of law raised are, thus, answered as under:

(i)     Section 292BB of the Act does not preclude an Assessee from raising
        an objection in any proceedings under the Act regarding non issuance
        of a notice under Section 143(2) of the Act, merely because the
        Assessee had appeared and cooperated during the reassessment
        proceedings without raising any objection with regard to non-issuance
        of the notice. and

(ii)    The revenue is not absolved of its obligation to serve a notice under
        Section 143(2) of the Act even if the Assessee requests that the earlier
        Return of Income filed under Section 139 of the Act be treated as the
        Return of Income filed in response to a notice under Section 148 of the
        Act . and

(iii)   Mere issuance of a letter by the Assessing Officer under section 142(1)
        of the Act during the course of reassessment proceedings, requiring the
        Assessee to explain the grounds on which re-assessment of income was
        proposed, does not amount to sufficient compliance of the mandatory


                                       12
      obligation to serve a notice under Section 143(2) of the Act.

24.    Consequently, we find no merit in the appeals, and the appeals are

accordingly dismissed.

23.     The High Court fell into error in treating an alleged
procedural irregularity as an automatic ground for grant of regular
bail, while completely ignoring the gravity of the offences under
Sections 339 and 940 of the OSA, 1923, and Sections 15241 and
23842(b) of the BNS, as well as the material collected during
investigation and placed on record. In the circumstances, we are
of the considered opinion that the High Court was not justified in
enlarging the Respondent on regular bail. The impugned judgment
and order cannot be sustained in law and is liable to be set aside.

any opinion on the merits of the allegations or the case. The
observations made hereinabove are confined exclusively to the
adjudication of the present appeal seeking cancellation of bail and
shall have no bearing whatsoever on the trial or the merits of the

                      Tribunal (AFT)1 and the High Court 2 granting War Injury Pension to the

3.    Facts, to the extent that they are relevant for disposal of this

appeal, are that the respondent was enrolled in the Indian Army on

30.12.1996. While being posted at Kargil w.e.f. 13.07.2003 to

06.07.2005,    he   was    diagnosed     with   ‘Rheumatoid     Arthritis

(Seropositive)’. Thereafter, he was also diagnosed with ‘PIVD L4/5,

L5/S1’ and ‘PIVD C5/C6 (Operated)’ while being posted at West

Bengal. The respondent applied for discharge and while discharging

him from service on 31.01.2013, the Release Medical Board conceded

to all the three disabilities of the respondent as aggravated by military

service @70% for life rounded off to 75% for life. Having rendered

more than 16 years of service, the respondent was granted Disability

Pension consisting of Service Element and Disability Element.

4.    Discharged in 2013, and having continued to regularly receive

pensionary benefits with Service Element as well as Disability

Element, it is after about 6 years that the respondent approached the

AFT seeking grant of War Injury Pension under Part II, Category E(i),

Para 4.1 of MoD Policy Letter (“Category E(i), Para 4.1 of MoD Policy

Letter”) dated 31.01.2001, instead of Disability pension for Rheumatoid

Arthritis (Seropositive), on the ground that this disablement is a direct

consequence of his posting at Kargil between 2003 to 2005.

5.    The Ministry of Defence (MoD), opposed the original application

on various grounds, principally on the ground that the respondent was
                                   2
not entitled to War Injury Pension as his disability was not covered

under Category E(i), Para 4.1 of MoD Policy Letter dated 31.01.2001.

It was also argued that while rounding off benefit was not admissible

with effect from 01.02.2013, respondent could claim the benefit of

rounding off benefits @75% disability with effect from 01.01.2016.

6.   By its order dated 08.04.2024, the AFT allowed the original

application holding that; (a) Rheumatoid Arthritis (Seropositive) has

originated in January, 2005 when the respondent served at Kargil

(J&K) 14F RAJ RIF, (b) the entire J&K area is an operational area and

therefore the stand of MoD that the disability was not caused due to

enemy action in an international war, peace keeping mission,

violence/attack by terrorist, border skirmishes etc. has no substance,

and that (c) the respondent made out a clear case for grant of War

Injury Element under Category E(i), Para 4.1 of MoD Policy Letter

dated 31.01.2001.

7.   Ministry of Defence’s challenge to the decision of AFT was

dismissed by the High Court on the ground that the opinion of the

Release    Medical   Board     proves   that   Rheumatoid     Arthritis

(Seropositive) originated when the respondent was actually posted at

Kargil between 2003 to 2005.




                                  3
8.    Learned Additional Solicitor General Ms. Archana Pathak Dave,

emphatically argued that respondent’s belated claim for the War Injury

Pension does not fall under Category E(i), Para 4.1 of MoD Policy

Letter. This is the short point for consideration and the answer to the

question depends upon what the MoD Policy Letter dated 31.01.2001

states.

9.    As usual, there is uncertainty about which Rules, Regulations,

Instructions and Policies of Ministry of Defence (MoD) are applicable.

We continue to wonder why this uncertainty about applicable rules

continues. It is high time that the MoD issues a comprehensive and

clearly identifiable subordinate legislation governing the services. This

is necessary for fairness in action and also for good governance.

10.   To start with, we may indicate that Para 4.1 of Part II of the MoD

Policy Letter dated 31.01.2001 is now also a part of the Pension

Regulations for Army, 2008. Chapter-IV of the Pension Regulations

deals with “Casualty Pensionary Awards when cause of Invalidment

from Service or Death is either Attributable to or Aggravated by Military

Service”. Regulation 82 of these Pension Regulations provides for

declaration of pensionary benefits on death and disability which is

attributable to or aggravated by Military Service under different

circumstances. The said Regulation formulates five categories, being


                                   4
categories ‘A’ to ‘E’, of which Category ‘E’ deals with pensionary

benefit in cases of death and disability arising out of nine

circumstances which are in the nature of an actual war or a war-like

situation. These are more or less in consonance with the MoD Policy

Letter dated 31.01.2001. However, learned ASG as well as the counsel

for the respondent have continued to refer and rely on the MoD Policy

Letter dated 31.01.2001, hence, we will also adopt the same method

to examine the legality of the claim of War Injury Pension, i.e. by

referring to the MoD Policy Letter.

11.   Part II of the Policy Letter deals with “Pensionary Benefits on

Death/Disability in Attributable/Aggravated Cases”. Under this Part,

there are five categories. Category ‘A’ deals with death and disability

due to natural causes neither attributable to nor aggravated by military

service. Category ‘B’ deals with cases where disease is attributable to

or aggravated by service conditions entitled to a disability pension.

Category ‘C’ deals with cases where death or disability occurs due to

accidents in the performance of duties, for which disability pension is

admissible. Category ‘D’ deals with cases where death or disability

occurs due to acts of violence, attack by terrorists, antisocial elements,

etc., whether on duty or not. Category ‘E’, with which we are

concerned, deals with death or disability arising out of nine


                                      5
circumstances. To examine this issue in detail, it is necessary to

reproduce Category ‘E’ as well as its sub-categories for ready

reference:-

         “Category E: Death or disability arising as a result of –

         (a) enemy action in international war.

         (b) action during deployment with a peace keeping mission
             abroad.
         (c) border skirmishes.
         (d) during laying or clearance of mines including enemy
             mines as also minesweeping operations.
         (e) On account of accidental explosions of mines while laying
             operationally oriented mine-field or lifting or negotiating
             mine-field laid by the enemy or own forces in operational
             areas near international borders or the line of control.
         (f) war like situations, including cases which are attributable
             to/aggravated by:-
             (i)    extremist acts, exploding mines etc., while on way
                    to an operational area
             (ii)   battle      inoculation  training    exercises    or
                    demonstration with live ammunition.
             (iii)  kit mapping by extremists while on operational
                    duty.
             (iv)   Flying operations in normal or (illegible) of war
                    plans and implementation of operations.
             (v)    (illegible)
         (g) An Act of violence by extremists, anti social elements etc
         while on operational duty.
         (h) Action against extremists, antisocial elements etc
         death/disability while employed in the aid of civil power in
         quelling agitation riots or revolt by demonstrators will be
         covered under this category.
         (i) Operations specially notified by the Govt. from time to
         time.”

12.   The contentious issue is about the scope and ambit of sub-

category E(i) relating to “Operations specially notified by the

Government from time to time”. While it has been the consistent stand


                                       6
of the respondent that posting at Kargil is based on operations

specially notified by the Government i.e. ‘Operation Rakshak’ and that

the disability occurred during posting at Kargil, MoD insists that

‘Operation Rakshak’ is not a specially notified operation under Para

4.1, Category E(i) and therefore, respondent’s Rheumatoid Arthritis

(Seropositive) cannot qualify as War Injury Pension.

13.   Reiterating the same stand, Ld. ASG submitted before us that if

such an interpretation is adopted, it will have the serious consequence

of ‘rendering other clauses in Category E otiose’ and also that every

army personnel posted in Jammu and Kashmir under Operation

Rakshak, would be entitled to War Injury Pension. It is the stand of

MoD that Category E(i) would cover only those operations, specially

notified by Government, such as Operation Sindoor or Operation Snow

Leopard etc., and not ongoing operations like Operation Rakshak

(covering entire J & K) or Operation Rhino (covering entire Assam).

Learned ASG also relied on Army Order 01 of 2003, Para 44 to support

the contention that in case of Battle Casualty, reports will not be

initiated in ongoing operations like Operation Rakshak or Operation

Rhino etc.

14.   On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondent insisted

that this Court should adopt the same reasoning as that of the AFT and

the High Court as Operation Rakshak at Kargil is an integral part of the
                                   7
“Operations specially notified by the Government from time to time”

under Category E(i) of the MoD Policy dated 31.01.2001. He also

submitted that many High Courts have taken a clear stand that War

Injury Pension is admissible for disabilities attributable to or arising out

of posting at such notified areas. Referring to the very same, Army

Order 1 of 2003, relied on by the ASG, it is submitted that Battle

Casualties are defined under Clauses 4 and 5 and the circumstances

for classification of Physical/Battle Casualties are mentioned in

Appendix ‘A’. He drew our attention to Clause (g) of Appendix ‘A’, to

show that Battle Casualties include casualties occurring while

operating on the International Border or Line of Control due to natural

calamities and illness caused by climatic conditions. On this basis, it is

submitted that respondent’s disability is directly attributable to the

climatic conditions at the Line of Control at Kargil.

15.   Having considered the matter in detail, we are of the opinion that

there is a distinction between each of the five categories contemplated

in Category E(i), Para 4.1 of MoD Policy Letter dated 31.01.2001. Of

the five categories, Category E is distinct and stands alone as it is

directly relatable to death or disability arising out of (a) enemy action

in international war, (b) action during deployment with a peacekeeping

mission abroad, (c) border skirmishes, (d) laying and clearing of mines

and minesweeping operations, (e) accidental explosions of mines etc.,
                                     8
(f) war-like situations due to extremist acts, battle inoculation, kit

mapping by extremists while on operational duty, flying operations, (g)

acts of violence by extremists, (h) action against extremists, antisocial

elements while agitation and riots, and finally (i) operations specially

notified by the Government from time to time. The sub-categories ‘a’

to ‘h’ clearly indicate egregious situations where the circumstances are

akin to war or extreme violence. These are instances where it can

clearly be expected that the army personnel posted in the area will be

faced with life-threatening situations. Moreover, instances under

Category E may not be exhaustive.

16.   Sub-Category E(i) is intended to give flexibility to our defence

administration as it is natural that all war-like situations cannot

comprehensively commence and conclude within the specified eight

Sub-Categories (a) to (h). Government has reserved to itself the

discretion to notify an additional sub-category (i) under Category E

from time to time, depending on the situation that may arise to initiate

an Operation for accomplishing a particular purpose. Going by the

plain language of the Policy, once a notification is issued for a specific

operation, Category E(i) is invoked, unless there is something

indicative either in the Policy or in the notification so issued. Except for

the oral statement of the Ld. ASG that Operation Rakshak is not

intended to be covered under Category E(i), there is no other
                                     9
interpretative aid for us to exclude Operation Rakshak from the scope

of Category E(i).

17.   There is no doubt about the fact that the power and jurisdiction

to prescribe applicability of a policy to the concerned personnel or the

conditions for its applicability are completely within the province of the

Defence Administration. However, the policy formulations must clearly

articulate their scope, ambit and their application. If an issue relating

to applicability of a policy arises for consideration, the primary burden

lies on the policymaker to demonstrate the circumstances in which the

benefit would accrue or not accrue. Normally, the policymaker’s

prescription will not be interfered with, unless the court finds that its

approach is beyond the range of reasonable meaning that can be

given to the plain language of the policy. If the policymaker interprets

its own policy against the plain language or in a manner that could be

discriminatory, arbitrary, irrational or goes against the very purpose

and object of the policy, the Courts will disregard the interpretation

offered by the policymaker.

18.   While interpreting the plain language of the policy, Courts will

simply declare, What a policy says, it is and not what is in the

imagination of the policymaker.

19.   We have already indicated that Category E(i), Para 4.1 of MoD

Policy Letter is intended to provide necessary discretion to include
                                   10
certain operations within the fold of the pensionary benefits arising out

of death or disability in certain war-like situations. Moreover, Sub-

category E(i) is enabling in nature. In other words, once operations

specially notified by the Government are issued as Sub-category (i)

does not indicate which of the operations specially notified by

Government fall outside the scope of Sub-category E(i), the policy will

apply and it must. When the language of the Policy is unrestrictive, it

is not the burden of the Court to limit its application through an

interpretative process, particularly when the policy relates to grant of

pensionary benefits. A liberal interpretation is compelling, and this

Court has adopted such an approach while interpreting such policies.

20.   Attempting to restrict the applicability of pensionary benefit under

Category E(i), the learned ASG relied on para 44 of the Army Order 01

of 2003 to submit that Battle Casualty reports will not be initiated in

ongoing operations like Operation Rakshak or Operation Rhino,

thereby wanting us to conclude that these are not operations falling

under Category E(i). At the first place, Army Order 1 of 2003 is

intended to deal with circumstances for classification of Physical and

Battle Casualties. This Army Order is relied on by the learned counsel

for the respondent to indicate that Battle Casualties are defined under

Clauses 4 and 5 and the circumstances for classification of

Physical/Battle Casualties are mentioned in Appendix ‘A’ of the said
                                   11
Order. Under Clause (g) of Appendix ‘A’, Battle Casualties are defined

to include casualties occurring while operating on the International

Border or Line of Control due to natural calamities like illness caused

by climatic conditions. On this basis, it is submitted that the

respondent’s disability is directly attributable to the climatic conditions

at the Line of Control at Kargil. We are of the opinion that it is

unnecessary to refer to and/or rely on Army Order 1 of 2003, as the

same causes more confusion than it clarifies. Moreover, MoD Policy

Letter dated 31.01.2001 is clear as when there is no distinction

between notifications issued under Category E(i), the benefit of the

said Policy Letter cannot be denied.

21.   For the reasons stated above, we see no reason to take a

different view from that of AFT or the High Court. At the same time, we

hasten to add that while notifying operations as contemplated under

Category E(i), the Government must declare in clear terms whether

the pensionary benefits contemplated under Para 4.1, Category E(i) of

the MoD Policy letter dated 31.01.2001 would be applicable to such

notification or not.

22.   In view of the above, Civil Appeal arising out of SLP (C) Diary

No. 27220 of 2026 against the judgment and order passed by the High

Court in CWP No. 23117 of 2025 dated 11.08.2025 is hereby

dismissed.
